Definitions & methods
Ethiopia · Nigeria · DRC

Discontinuation and switching extensions

National reasons and timing are followed by post-discontinuation pathways and the separate analysis of partner/spousal disapproval.

Which actionable reasons contribute most, and when?

These figures describe the first 12 months after method initiation. All estimates use modern-method episodes excluding EC. Potentially actionable causes are method failure, wanting a more effective method, bleeding changes, other side effects/health, and access/cost/convenience. Partner/spousal disapproval is separate and is excluded from these five categories.

How to read the figures: The horizontal axis is a percentage, not months. A full bar gives the 12-month probability of ending for that reason. Gold shows the portion accumulated by month 3; the other colors show the added probability during months 4–6, 7–9 and 10–12. The right-hand percentage divides the month-3 probability by its month-12 value. It is a timing summary, not a discontinuation rate.

For example, Ethiopia’s bleeding-related probability is 1.08% by month 3 and 2.81% by month 12. Thus, 38.5% of its first-year bleeding-related risk has accumulated by month 3, calculated using unrounded estimates.

All three figures use the same 0–8% horizontal scale and display weighted point estimates. Nonactionable endings remain competing events. The charts describe when method endings occur, not when symptoms begin. These estimates do not show intervention effects or net losses of modern users after switching/restarting.

Ethiopia: reasons and timing of potentially actionable discontinuation

The combined 12-month probability for these five categories is 16.97%. Each bar shows one reason’s contribution to that probability.

What happens after an actionable modern-method ending?

What these figures tell us

Stopping a method does not always mean stopping modern contraception. A woman may move straight to another method, spend some time without one, or return to use later. These figures follow what happened after women stopped a modern method for one of the potentially actionable reasons.

They help us answer the following questions:

  • Which methods were women using when they stopped? The first column shows the methods that ended. Its percentages describe these discontinuations, not the method mix among all current users.
  • What happened soon afterward? The month-1 column shows how often an ending was followed by modern use, no method, traditional use, or a pregnancy-related record.
  • What changed over the following year? The ribbons connect each ending to the same woman’s later records. They show, for example, whether women recorded with no method at an earlier snapshot were using a modern method later.
  • Where did things stand twelve months after stopping? The final column shows the share in each recorded state at that point. Modern use includes a different modern method or a return to the original one.

Two women can reach the same month-12 outcome through very different experiences. One might switch straight from injectables to pills and keep using them. Another might spend several months without a method before starting an implant. Both count as modern users at month 12. The earlier columns help show that difference.

We should read the ribbons as links between the displayed months. A woman recorded in modern use at months 3 and 6 could still have had a gap between those snapshots. The figures also do not tell us which subsequent method lasts longest, or why a woman did or did not return to use. Answering those questions requires looking at the intervening monthly records and subsequent method episodes.

Who is included, and when does follow-up start?

The preceding charts measure the probability of an ending during the first twelve months after method initiation. The following alluvials start with episodes that have already ended for a potentially actionable cause and describe what follows. They include endings at any duration of method use, rather than only first-year endings.

First column: the method recorded in the episode’s last month of use. Later columns: the same endings linked to recorded states 1, 3, 6 and 12 months afterward. All percentages use the country’s entire eligible follow-up cohort as the denominator. A month-12 modern-use percentage therefore combines all original methods.

These figures describe twelve months after discontinuation. The mCPR planning sensitivity tables instead assess modern use twelve months from the prediction baseline, allowing less post-ending time for women who discontinue later in that window. The two quantities are not interchangeable.

Ethiopia: what follows an actionable modern-method ending?

1,799 observed endings from 1,531 women, each with twelve subsequent calendar months available. Original-method EC episodes are excluded. Only potentially actionable endings are included.

Reading the month-12 column: 41.6% of the weighted eligible endings across all original methods combined are followed by modern use twelve months later. Modern use can reflect a different method or restarting the original method.

Does subsequent use differ by the reason for stopping?

The alluvials combine all actionable reasons. These charts take the next step: they link the reported reason for stopping to the following year of contraceptive records.

For example, the bleeding row asks: among eligible endings attributed to bleeding changes, how many are followed by modern use throughout the year, a return after an interruption, or another recorded state at month 12? The access row asks the same question among access-, cost- or convenience-related endings.

Each row has its own denominator and sums to 100%. These are outcome distributions among endings, not discontinuation probabilities. The gold segment can include pregnancy-related or traditional-use months before modern use is recorded at month 12. Method failure remains separate because pregnancy caused the original ending.

These comparisons help show where later modern use is less common and where return follows an interruption. They do not establish why those differences occur or which service response would change them.

Ethiopia: subsequent use by reason for stopping

The overall row uses the same 1,799 endings as the alluvial. Each subsequent row includes only endings attributed to the reason shown. All original modern methods are combined.

How to read a row: the five colors divide that reason’s eligible endings into their subsequent histories and month-12 states. Teal means a modern method was recorded in every following month. Gold means modern use at month 12 after earlier months outside modern use. The remaining colors show no method, a pregnancy-related record, or traditional use at month 12. Teal plus gold gives the percentage in the right-hand column.

Which modern methods do women take up after stopping?

The preceding bar graphs show continuity and status at month 12. These matrices describe a different part of the experience: the first modern method recorded at any point during the twelve months after a potentially actionable ending.

For example, an injectable ending followed by pills, then an implant, then no method at month 12 is assigned to the Pill column here. In the alluvial, the same ending appears in the No method category at month 12. Both descriptions can be true.

These tables show which alternatives women actually adopt and how often there is no modern return during the year. They do not show how long the new method lasts. Partner/spousal disapproval is excluded from the actionable ending cohort. The unit is a method ending; one woman can contribute more than one ending.

Ethiopia: first modern method used within 12 months after discontinuation

The same 1,799 potentially actionable endings from 1,531 women are followed here as in the alluvial and preceding bar graph.

Read across one row: start with the method that ended. The columns show the first modern method recorded in any of the next twelve months, whether immediately or after a gap or pregnancy. Every ending appears in just one column. An ending stays assigned to that first modern method even if it is later discontinued.

What is the denominator? Each method row includes all eligible actionable endings of that original method, including endings with no modern return. The gold overall row combines all original methods. Percentages sum to 100% within each row before rounding.

How this differs from the alluvial: 55.3% of these endings are followed by modern use at least once during the year, while 41.6% are followed by modern use at month 12. The matrix describes the first destination; the alluvial describes states at specific follow-up months. The 44.7% in “No modern return” have no modern method recorded in any of the twelve following months. This is broader than “No method” and differs from being outside modern use only at month 12.

Separate partner/spousal analysis
Ethiopia · Nigeria · DRC

Modern-method discontinuation due to partner/spousal disapproval

First-year probabilities and timing, pooled across modern methods and shown by method.

EC is excluded from all episode denominators. Partner/spousal disapproval is analyzed separately from potentially actionable causes. All other method-ending reasons remain competing events.

Ethiopia

Among eligible modern-method episodes, the estimated probability of ending the original method because of reported partner/spousal disapproval within its first year is 0.57%. Other reasons for ending the method are competing events.

What share of discontinuations is attributed to partner/spousal disapproval?

1.49% of observed modern-method discontinuations occurring within the first year were attributed to partner/spousal disapproval. The denominator includes endings for all reasons, including other, unknown and missing reasons. EC is excluded.

Definitions and methods

Population and outcome

The analysis uses women’s individual recode data and prepared contraceptive-calendar episodes for Ethiopia 2024–25, Nigeria 2024, and DRC 2023–24. The observation window is 3–62 months before each woman’s interview. Episodes have an identifiable start; eligible delayed entry is retained. Modern-method episodes are included and emergency contraception (EC) is excluded throughout.

The outcome is an original-method ending within 12 months of initiation whose reported main reason is husband/partner disapproval (calendar reason code 3). Partner/spousal disapproval is a separate outcome and is not included among potentially actionable causes. These estimates do not describe broader partner influence or spousal support.

Competing-risk life tables

At each month, the weighted number of target endings is divided by the weighted original-method risk set. That monthly probability is multiplied by the probability of still using the original method at the beginning of the month and accumulated over time. Every other method-ending reason reduces original-method survival as a competing event. Episodes ending for other reasons are retained in the analysis.

Risk sets change as episodes end, become censored, or enter observation after initiation. Therefore, a 12-month probability is not calculated by dividing observed endings by the total episode count. Repeated episodes are allowed. The point estimates were independently checked against a weighted Aalen–Johansen estimator and a separate life-table implementation.

Subgroup estimates and sample support

Age and parity are reconstructed at method initiation. Parity counts live births occurring by that month; the order of events within a month is unknown. Full birth-history counts were checked against total births reported at interview. Residence is measured at interview. Every characteristic partitions the full eligible cohort, and subgroup episode and event counts reconcile with the national totals. These are unadjusted subgroup probabilities; they retain actual differences in method mix. No formal subgroup tests or minimum-detectable-difference calculations were performed.

Share among discontinuations

The reason share divides weighted partner-disapproval endings by all weighted observed modern-method endings within their first 12 months, in the same eligible episode cohort. This is a conditional distribution among observed endings, rather than a life-table probability. Other, unknown and missing reasons stay in the denominator. Reason-share intervals use the same full-frame survey bootstrap as the life-table estimates. The cumulative-risk timing shares shown elsewhere divide life-table probability increments by their 12-month probability and have a different denominator.

Weights and survey uncertainty

Point estimates use the women’s DHS sampling weights. Percentile 95% confidence intervals use 1,999 stratified Rao–Wu n−1 cluster-bootstrap replicates drawn from the full interviewed-women survey frame, including clusters without eligible episodes. Women and all their episodes stay together within each sampled cluster. A small positive multiplier (0.0001) preserves sparse risk-set support; its effect is removed from replicate deviations before calculating intervals.

No interval is reported when no target event was observed by the specified month; an all-zero empirical bootstrap would give misleading certainty. The sample flags are transparent descriptive screening rules, not proof of sufficient power. No model-based smoothing, adjusted regression, or pairwise significance tests were used.

Interpretation and limitations

  • The life-table probabilities and the reason shares are explicitly labeled and have different denominators. Neither measures the percentage of women who experience partner opposition or the probability that a current user will leave modern use next year.
  • Switching or restarting after an ending does not erase that ending. This module does not estimate net loss of modern users or an effect on mCPR.
  • Rare events, retrospective recall, monthly date resolution, a single reported main reason, and differences in method mix affect interpretation. Broad Other-modern estimates combine heterogeneous methods.
  • Country and method estimates should be read with their intervals and counts. No causal explanation or statistical ranking follows from their point estimates alone.
